items.title: NASA’s Swift Observatory has burned up in the atmosphere – the indispensable telescope helped astronomers track fast-moving events in space
items.abstract: The Swift Observatory allowed astronomers to study events that happen quickly in the universe, such as stars exploding.
paras: A 22-year-old space telescope lost its fight against gravity and came crashing down to Earth on the morning of Nov. 4, 2026, above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory had been the go-to telescope for observing astrophysical events that happen quickly, such as supernovas . Its onboard instruments allowed it to contribute greatly to many subfields of science.
Swift was not classified as a flagship observatory, like the Hubble Space Telescope or Chandra X-Ray Observatory , but it left behind a legacy that will not swiftly be forgotten.

The Swift Observatory first came onto the scene in 2004 when NASA launched it into low Earth orbit . Originally called the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, its purpose was to move quickly to follow up on explosive events called gamma-ray bursts and their afterglows using its three onboard telescopes.

Swift’s name is not an acronym. Instead, it refers to its speed and likens the observatory to the bird . It could rotate and move quickly to observe transient events , which are events that happen quickly and fade away.
Watching for gamma-ray bursts

Gamma-ray bursts are the most explosive and energetic events in the universe. Scientists theorize they come from the explosions of large stars or mergers of a very dense type of star called neutron stars . Gamma-ray bursts, as the name implies, release large bursts of gamma-rays, but as these explosions fade, they lose energy. Scientists can spot remnants of gamma-ray bursts by looking for X-rays and optical light as the gamma rays themselves fade.

Swift’s burst alert telescope could see light in the gamma-ray portion of the electromagnetic spectrum , so it searched directly for gamma-ray bursts. Its X-ray telescope and ultraviolet-optical telescope could measure the resulting afterglow of X-ray and UV light these events produced as they faded.

What set Swift apart was its ability to do what’s called slewing: In order to follow up on transient events, it swiveled its telescopes around quickly and could cover 50 degrees in less than 75 seconds . Comparatively, it takes Hubble about 15 minutes to turn 90 degrees .
By 2015, just 10 years after science operations started, Swift detected its 1,000th gamma-ray burst .
Beyond gamma-ray bursts

Swift’s ability to slew quickly allowed it to detect more than just gamma-ray bursts. Its onboard instruments could detect anything that changes quickly in the sky, including supernovae and X-ray flares from binary stars , which are two stars bound by gravity that tend to interact with each other. It could also detect the electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational waves , which result from large distortions in space-time, such as the merger of dense objects such as black holes and neutron stars.

In 2008, when observing another supernova, Swift by chance detected a slight rise in X-rays , which preceded a supernova explosion. This initial increase in X-rays represented the earliest phase of supernova evolution ever observed. Swift’s extensive alert network notified astronomers all over the world who were able to point other space- and ground-based telescopes at the supernova to follow up and obtain even more data.

Then in 2017, when the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – whose principal investigator Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics – detected high-energy neutrinos , Swift was able to help localize their source. Neutrinos are massless particles that do not interact with most matter. This property makes it hard for physicists to detect them and pinpoint their source. Scientists know that astrophysical events can emit them, and they used Swift to connect these neutrinos to a very energetic supermassive black hole at the center of its galaxy .

In 2025, Swift detected a compound called hydroxyl on the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS , indicating the presence of water. This result may help answer the question of how Earth obtained water on its surface. Some theories propose that comets and interstellar objects bombarded the Earth in the early solar system and deposited water.
A failed recovery mission

Swift’s journey took a turn in 2024 and 2025, as the Sun became more active . These years were in a period known as a solar maximum , when more solar flares, or explosions on the surface of the Sun, released matter and high-energy particles that hit Earth’s atmosphere .

Because of this increase in space weather, many people as far south as Pennsylvania were able to see the northern lights. While this activity produced jaw-dropping views, it also exerted pressure on satellites. Solar particles can exert a small force on whatever they hit, and when there are many, that force multiplies.

This force pushed against Swift, which lived in low Earth orbit at about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface. The telescope eventually reentered the atmosphere, where drag pulled it down toward Earth.
NASA partnered with a company called Katalyst Space Technologies and launched a mission to boost Swift back into its orbit on July 3, 2026.

Unfortunately, this mission failed, and Swift reentered and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere in early November. The observatory didn’t hit the surface fully intact. Instead, it mostly burned up on its way in.

The loss of such an observatory is a tough blow to the astronomical community, which was gearing up to use the satellite in conjunction with the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory . However, astronomers will continue to remember Swift’s team and their countless accomplishments and discoveries.
Editor’s note: This article was updated on Nov. 4, 2026, to reflect when and where Swift reentered the atmosphere.

items.title: How space weather powers auroras in the sky and threatens power grids on the ground
items.abstract: When an aurora lights up the sky, electric currents can also flow through the ground beneath your feet.
paras: An aurora is one of nature’s most spectacular light shows: It looks like green or red curtains rippling across the night sky. When viewed from the ground, this colorful display might seem far away and disconnected from anything happening on Earth’s surface.

But while these beautiful displays are part of a much larger process known as “space weather” – changes in Earth’s space environment caused by activity from the Sun – they’re closely connected to electric currents that can flow through the ground under your feet.

Space weather can create a spectacle in the sky, while also driving electric currents that can damage power grids and other technological systems on the ground. Space physicists like us want to understand how space weather can affect infrastructure on Earth.

Our research shows that a single space weather event called a substorm , during which energy is released tens of thousands of miles away from Earth, can affect the ground within minutes. The strength of the impact can vary from place to place depending on the latitude and the structure of the soil and rock below your feet.
From solar storm to substorm
Earth is constantly immersed in the solar wind : a stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun. Occasionally, the Sun releases a much larger eruption called a coronal mass ejection .

This cloud of charged particles and magnetic fields does not simply “hit” Earth and immediately cause power-grid failures. Instead, it can set off a chain of processes in space that can pose a threat to power grids .

First, when the coronal mass ejection reaches Earth, the charged particles and magnetic fields it carries interact with Earth’s magnetosphere . The magnetosphere is the region of space around Earth dominated by its magnetic field.

If the coronal mass ejection’s magnetic field is oriented in a certain way, it can connect with Earth’s magnetic field on the side facing the Sun. The solar wind then carries these connected field lines around Earth away from the Sun and stretches them far out into space behind Earth. This process forms a long region of stretched magnetic field lines called the magnetotail.

Magnetic energy builds up in the magnetotail as the solar wind continues to push the field lines farther into space – until they come close enough to reconnect . Then, the stored energy is released in an explosive process known as a substorm . This release occurs on the side of Earth facing away from the Sun, roughly 28,000 to 40,000 miles (45,000 to 65,000 kilometers) from Earth.

During the substorm, energetic particles shoot along the magnetic field lines toward Earth. When these particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere, about 56 to 93 miles (90 to 150 kilometers) overhead, they produce the glowing aurora.
These energetic particles also drive strong electrical currents in Earth’s upper atmosphere . Rapid changes in these currents can cause Earth’s magnetic field at the ground level to change sharply.
These changing magnetic fields can induce electric currents in the ground and in power lines, potentially damaging transformers and tripping circuit breakers.
From the magnetotail to Earth’s surface
Our team wanted to find out how closely the aurora is linked to disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field and how long it takes for a disturbance released in the magnetotail to reach Earth’s surface.

We examined two auroral events in detail by combining data from NASA spacecraft – including THEMIS, time history of events and macroscale interactions during substorms , and NOAA’s GOES, geostationary operational environmental satellites – with data from a dense network of magnetometers across Arctic Canada that measure changes in Earth’s magnetic field at the ground. These changes in the magnetic field can drive electric currents in the ground and power lines.

The observations revealed a clear sequence. When these stretched magnetic field lines on the nightside suddenly reconnected, the spacecraft recorded an abrupt change in the magnetic field and a burst of charged particles moving toward Earth. About seven minutes later, the magnetic field at the ground began to change rapidly. The effects of this energy release, tens of thousands of miles away, reached Earth’s surface within minutes.
The aurora and ground disturbance do not appear everywhere at once. In our observations, they began at lower latitudes and then spread toward the North Pole over the next 20 to 30 minutes.

Nearby geomagnetic stations, however, often recorded very different responses. Stations tens to hundreds of miles apart could see strong magnetic swings at one site and weak ones at another. The difference depended on the strength of currents in Earth’s upper atmosphere and local conditions – including how electrically conductive the upper atmosphere is overhead and how conductive the ground beneath the magnetic station is. This atmospheric conductivity can vary with sunlight and auroral activity, while ground conductivity depends on local geology and moisture levels.
Seeing a spectacular aurora does not automatically mean the ground beneath it is experiencing the strongest magnetic disturbances or electric currents.
When the aurora becomes a grid problem

History shows that space weather poses a real risk to space and ground infrastructure. During a March 1989 geomagnetic storm, people witnessed spectacular auroras as far south as Texas, while rapid changes in magnetic fields contributed to the collapse of the Hydro-Québec power system . More than 6 million people lost electricity for about nine hours on a cold winter night. With the city lights extinguished, the aurora appeared even more spectacular.

A similar combination occurred during the Halloween storms of October 2003. Auroras illuminated skies across Europe, while geomagnetically induced currents contributed to a blackout affecting about 50,000 people in Malmö, Sweden.

Recently, during the May 2024 geomagnetic storm – the strongest in over two decades – geomagnetically induced currents stressed the power grid in southern Sweden, forcing a transmission link to disconnect and temporarily interrupting the flow of electricity through that part of the grid.

Space weather forecasts can warn power grid operators hours before solar activity reaches Earth, giving them time to monitor grid conditions and prepare for possible disruptions. But the effects of substorms, including potential risks to power grids, develop after the solar wind interacts with Earth’s magnetic environment. Our research shows that these effects unfold on timescales of minutes.

The next time the aurora ripples across the night sky, remember that the colorful light shining overhead is only one part of a larger process. Tens of thousands of miles away, an explosive release of magnetic energy may have just taken place. Within minutes, its effects can begin to reach the ground.
The beauty of the aurora and the risk of power-grid disruption from invisible currents above and below are two faces of the same space weather event.

items.title: Are schools a great equalizer? They help kids catch up, but wealthier children still pull ahead
items.abstract: By some measures, schools are a great equalizer for children coming from different backgrounds. But this isn’t the full story.
paras: In 1848, the education reformer Horace Mann called public schooling “the great equalizer of the conditions of men.” More than 175 years later, education scholars are still arguing about whether he was right.

Some research finds that a child’s family background shapes their academic achievement far more than schools do . Other work finds that schools narrow academic achievement gaps that would otherwise be even wider .

A classic study following Baltimore children in the 1980s found that low-income and wealthier kids learned at similar rates during the school year . Achievement gaps grew over the summer, when some children read with parents, visited libraries and went to camp, while others didn’t have those same opportunities. How much summer learning loss exists is still an open question.

But the larger point holds: Gaps between rich and poor children in reading and math skills are already large on the first day of kindergarten , driven by factors outside of K-12 schooling. For a given group of students, those gaps then stay about the same size through the school years.
I am a scholar of education policy who studies the different factors that shape students’ learning, including teachers and the quality of their instruction.

Instead of measuring how much students learn at school, as is often the case, my colleagues and I recently measured what students receive in and out of school : the school funding, education support services and time that schools, government programs and families put into each child.
By some measures, schools really are an equalizer for children from different backgrounds – but this finding has its limits.
A gap that starts early in childhood

In our 2026 study , we combined data from 10 nationally representative government surveys to track 77 kinds of investments, as we call them, that contribute to raising and educating children. This includes teachers, tutoring, housing, food and childcare. We also measured factors that don’t have a direct cost, such as the time parents and caregivers spend reading with children.
We put a dollar value on each factor – valuing parents’ time at the average U.S. hourly wage, for example – so we could add them up and compare what children from different backgrounds receive.
Counting government investment, family spending and the time parents spend with their children, the average child in the U.S. receives about US$502,000 from birth to age 18, our analysis shows.
The gaps in how much different children receive start early.
Before age 5, children from the poorest fourth of families receive about $44,000 less in total investments than children from the richest fourth – marking a gap of 24%.
Most of that early difference comes from housing and childcare costs.
However, a striking pattern emerges as children transition into elementary school. The gap in total investment between the richest and poorest children is cut in half, from 24% to 12%.
For Black children, the benefit of starting school is even greater. Investment gaps between Black and white children shrink from 20% in early childhood years to 7% once kindergarten begins.
This matters because research shows that more school spending improves students’ achievement and long-term outcomes , especially for those from low-income families .
So why don’t achievement gaps close during the school years?
Catching up vs. getting ahead
Part of the answer is what money buys.

Our research shows that once children are in school, those from the lowest-income families receive 72% more in tutoring and 68% more in special education than those from the highest-income families, and Black children receive more than twice as much tutoring as white children.
These services are meant to help students catch up. A dollar spent catching up is not the same as a dollar spent getting ahead.

Tutoring has long been one of schools’ main catch-up tools, and since the pandemic, schools have leaned on it more than ever . It’s a reasonable bet. Studies that randomly assign students to tutoring find some of the largest test-score gains of any school program .

Schools serving many low-income students have long been able to use federal Title I money for tutoring . Pandemic relief money made a bigger push possible. Congress sent schools nearly $190 billion , and the largest round was divided among districts the same way as Title I money , so high-poverty districts got more.

By 2022-23, more than a third of public schools offered “ high-dosage” tutoring , meaning frequent sessions in small groups. Schools serving more low-income students and students of color were more likely to offer it .
But for many low-income, Black and Latino students, tutoring wasn’t new.

In our data, collected from 2014 to 2021, about 17% of school-age children were being tutored, including 25% of Black children and 19% of Latino children, compared with 14% of white children. For Black, Latino and low-income children who received tutoring, over 75% got that support from public schools.

Early in the recovery, at least, the share of students getting tutoring didn’t appear to grow much. A nationally representative survey of parents in fall 2022 found about 15% of students were being tutored.

Meanwhile, the pandemic widened achievement gaps. Students in high-poverty districts still trail those in wealthier districts by more than students in the same grades did before the pandemic. Schools leaned harder on catch-up help that low-income, Black and Latino students were already getting. Federal relief money did help high-poverty districts recover . But even with that help, gaps remain wider than before the pandemic.
Who gets ahead
Catch-up help is only half the picture. Wealthier children also get more of the resources that help them pull ahead, in school and out.

Some studies show, for example, that low-income students and students of color are more likely than richer, white students to have newer, less experienced teachers . Our study documents the same pattern.
The differences are even starker outside of school.
In our data, wealthier families invest far more in music lessons, sports and other activities that can help kids get ahead.

Related research shows that by 2024, the richest 10% of families spent more than 13 times as much per child as the poorest quarter on childcare, education and extracurricular activities – up from about three times as much in the early 1980s.
Equal spending isn’t enough
Our findings show that public education is the main reason the investment gap between rich and poor children shrinks once kids turn 5.

But equal spending is not equal opportunity. Much of the extra school spending on low-income, Black and Latino children goes to making up for gaps that opened before they started school. Meanwhile, wealthier children keep getting more of the experienced teachers and enrichment that help them pull ahead.

If schools are going to be a true equalizer – closing gaps, not just keeping them from growing – more catch-up help won’t be enough on its own. These students also need more of what helps their wealthier peers get ahead. And because the widest gaps open before kindergarten – in housing and childcare, where public support is thinnest – closing them can’t be left to schools alone.

items.title: Short supplies of crucial equipment stymie changes to US electricity grid
items.abstract: Whether you want renewable energy, fossil fuel power plants, data centers or reduced storm vulnerability, it will require equipment that’s hard to make out of materials that are hard to get.
paras: Americans have a lot of plans for the country’s power grid. Some people want to expand renewable energy by building solar and wind farms . Others want to add new coal- or natural gas-fired power plants . There are those who want to provide power to some unknown number of data centers processing artificial intelligence algorithms.

To accomplish any of these goals, the country will need a significant number of pieces of equipment whose design was invented in the late 19th century: large power transformers . These giant metal structures are about the size of a two-story house and weigh as much as 400 tons – roughly equivalent to a fully loaded Boeing 747 . They convert high voltages used to transmit electricity down to voltage levels people can use in their homes and businesses. And they are made largely in the same way they were when they were invented 150 years ago .

Many of the large power transformers in service in the U.S. and around the world are aging beyond their intended lifespans . And there aren’t enough replacements to meet the world’s needs. It can take more than three years for a company’s order to be filled and delivered.
Transformers as transport systems

Large power transformers are crucial to transporting electricity over long distances . Power plants – whether coal- or gas-fired, hydropower dams, or solar or wind farms – are often far from the customers who need the electricity that’s generated.

Transmitting power through wires generates heat , which over a long distance dramatically reduces the amount of energy arriving at the far end. To reduce energy losses, power companies use large transformers to increase the voltage. You can think of this like freight being loaded onto large trucks and directed over interstate highways. They can carry a lot of energy more efficiently than smaller cars could on smaller roads.

But the high-voltage power is not safe for a home or business to use right away, just as a semitruck at highway speeds shouldn’t try to enter your driveway. So when the power arrives near a group of customers, it needs to take an off-ramp, going through another large transformer that lowers its voltage to levels regular customers can use. Then low-voltage lines act as local city streets, delivering the electricity the short distance from the highway exit to homes and businesses.

Between 2019 and 2025, demand for generator step-up transformers, those that connect power plants to the transmission grid, nearly tripled . And over the same period, demand for transformers to work as off-ramps more than doubled, with costs increasing 80% .

These devices are not mass-produced from automated assembly lines. They are custom-engineered to meet specific needs and demands for their intended destinations. If a specialized transformer fails during an extreme storm or heat wave, there aren’t just replacements waiting in a warehouse somewhere.
The supply chain trap
What these transformers are made of is a big part of the delay.

One key ingredient is what’s known as grain-oriented electrical steel . This is not at all average steel. It is manufactured using precise thermal and mechanical processes that position the steel’s magnetic crystals in a single direction. The crystalline alignment allows magnetic fields to pass through the metal with low energy loss, which is crucial for handling large amounts of electricity. However, only a handful of specialized steel mills worldwide have the technology to produce it. Just one mill is in the U.S.
Also in short supply is copper , which is made into wires that are wrapped around the core of the transformer , typically made of steel, to achieve the correct voltage adjustment.
Work-around has its own problems

Because of the transformer shortage, it can take utilities and power producers more than two years to get equipment to connect new power plants to the grid – regardless of whether they are powered by nuclear energy, fossil fuels, solar energy or the wind.

To get around that delay, companies that run data centers to power artificial intelligence systems have sought to bypass the grid altogether, by installing dedicated, on-site natural gas power plants to run the computer centers.

That move has caused another supply chain problem . Gas turbines burn at over 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,100 C), which is hot enough to melt standard steel. Turbine blades are manufactured with a complicated process out of very specialized combinations of metal and coated with ceramic heat shields .

As tech companies have placed more and larger orders, the time between ordering a gas turbine and having it delivered has stretched to between three and seven years . And prices in 2027 are expected to be nearly triple what they were in 2019 , due to the increase in demand and still-rare materials.
What can be done?
A supply chain built in the 19th century is struggling to reliably serve power to the 21st-century economy.
Large power transformers are also key to upgrading the existing grid and reducing its vulnerability to large storms or extended outages .
The solutions are both concrete and complicated.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has recommended standardizing transformer designs , rather than having each be custom-built. That would allow manufacturers to produce more units more quickly, with an assembly line-style process. It would also allow utility companies to share emergency spares.

The U.S. Department of Energy has recommended deploying what are collectively called “ grid-enhancing technologies .” These methods include sensors that monitor in real time exactly how much power can be transmitted through long-distance wires and advanced software that can find alternative routes by which to distribute electricity from power plants to maximize what’s available to customers. Together, these types of systems can allow the transmission of 15% to 20% more electricity than without them, easing bottlenecks while waiting for new transformers to be delivered.
Longer term, the U.S. could produce more grain-oriented electrical steel, process more copper and expand its capacity to build large power transformers.
All the ways people want to adapt, improve, expand and modernize the power grid are dependent on this one type of equipment. Without large power transformers, none of the efforts will get very far.

In a sense, leaders face a choice either way: solve these hardware shortages or accept the default consequences of grid congestion, delayed projects and rising costs. Resolving the transformer bottleneck would be what turns that passive reality into active choice.

items.title: ‘Epic’ blue wave helps Democrats take Congress in overwhelming rebuke to President Trump
items.abstract: Election Day turned into a massive rebuke of President Donald Trump: a blue wave not seen in 20 years that was built on transforming the economy and rising prices into a central line of attack.
paras: Voters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions , including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago .

Democrats took control of the House and Senate , flipping Senate seats in Texas , South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed.
The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections .

It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida?

There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win , and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought.

It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats.

Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district . What does that tell you?

It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties.

It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts.

I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump.

I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections.

That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending?

Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns.

This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day.

And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton . And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes.
Any final thoughts?

The territory that Democrats covered is unbelievable. The South Carolina Senate race went to Annie Andrews , the Democrat, which was unfathomable even a few months ago. Mississippi still appears to be somewhat in play. The blue wave turned into something approaching a tsunami. I think a lot of Democrats saw the polling and didn’t want to believe it or couldn’t bring themselves to believe it. But some of this late polling seems to have gotten things on the mark.

What we’ve seen in these midterm elections is a massive rebuke of the last two years of the Trump administration, and a sort of blue wave of epic proportions toward the Democrats, the likes of which we haven’t seen in 20 or more years. It’s a huge confirmation of the approach that Democrats took in this election.

items.title: Tracing the recruitment trap behind Russia’s war
items.abstract: Bangladeshi men paid agents for Russian jobs and ended up on the front lines. Families wait for bodies and answers, and they want the recruiters behind it in a courtroom.
paras: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation , he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine . He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten , he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries . Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines .
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation ( ORF ). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted , while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy . Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds . Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit ( RMMRU ), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training ( BMET ) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited ( BOESL ) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe ; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.

Egypt’s crackdown on independent media reaches Mada Masr as editor faces trial
items.abstract: Egypt has convicted Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief Lina Attalah and ordered the outlet closed, weeks after arresting the whole Matsada2sh newsroom.
paras: Egypt convicted Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations, and ordered it closed
Originally published on Global Voices
Lina Attalah. Photo from Mada Masr website, used with permission.
A crackdown on independent media in Egypt is escalating.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh , a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.

The six-person team was forcibly disappeared , illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news. They remain in pretrial detention.

The crackdown then reached Mada Masr , one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah. On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.

The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license, in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial. She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later. The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.

According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected. The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.

Mada Masr was founded in 2013 as an independent, critical, investigative outlet. In another decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region. It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.

Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism. At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday, October 30, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.” A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.

“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about. But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads. It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.” It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.

In an op-ed published on October 26, the Mada Masr team wrote that “in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday.”

They added: “There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism.”

And: “We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small us, Mada Masr, but a much bigger we.”

In Egypt, journalists who documented torture, political imprisonment, and security crackdowns now face courts that process them quickly and unfairly, under a licensing scheme that has left applicants without an answer for years.
For journalism to be free, that licensing scheme and its chilling effects on access to information, knowledge production, and critical voices in Egypt and beyond must be stopped.

How We’re Covering the Midterms — and the Aftermath
items.abstract: The post How We’re Covering the Midterms — and the Aftermath appeared first on ProPublica .
paras: This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums . Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines . President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious.

Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger?

As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future.

ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?

And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections.

We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching . But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months.
Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history.

We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”

Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties , typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election.

One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell , a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts . But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to.

We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “​​​​What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate.

We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise.

Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign.

Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins , the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn , a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year.

Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. Graham’s communications director wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior … are simply false.” The FBI stopped examining the allegations after Trump purged the bureau. Our coverage likewise has become an issue in the Maine race.

We stand at a moment of uncertainty in our history as a democracy. Trump has made his willingness to smear news organizations an essential aspect of his appeal. He routinely insults reporters to their face and has attempted to ban some outlets from the White House and Air Force One because he didn’t like the stories they wrote about him. He has diverted hundreds of federal agents from their jobs fighting drug cartels and organized crime to search for evidence that noncitizens have illegally voted in federal elections. Hardly any were found .

I’m deeply reluctant to make any predictions about how all this will end. ProPublica prepared for an array of dire scenarios in November of 2024 that might arise from a close election. None of them came to pass as Trump decisively prevailed. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit to block the Alaska Senate race results over the weekend, and the Trump administration’s plans to appeal stand on shaky legal ground.
The one thing I know for certain is that we will keep digging into the story of what really happened in this election, whoever wins.

I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
items.abstract: The post I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining. appeared first on ProPublica .
paras: Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.

The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.

The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.

Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?

In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks . Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided . The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.

The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”

My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster.

When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.
While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously.

Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.

Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?

In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.

Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year.
But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.

There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.
I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.

Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle.

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “ Rule of Law Index 2026 ” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice. That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific. Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score). Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth).

In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests. However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations.

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report , which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector. Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights. Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.
Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score).

Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026. The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020 , which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges. Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred. Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

The report described the “constraints in government’s power” performance as moderately to alarmingly risky, with constraints from the legislature ranking 84, judiciary 64, independent auditing and review bodies 61, non-government organizations 105, and the law 90 — the law refers to the legal framework that protects procedural justice and integrity regarding the appointment of officials and the electoral process. As for the subfactor “official sanctioned for misconduct,” which has a fair 22 ranking, some Hongkongers may consider the score too generous given that only one official has taken responsibility and resigned over the preventable Taipo Fire disaster.

A similar downward trend appears in the “fundamental rights” category, which ranked 29th in 2015, slipped to 38th in 2020, plummeted to 54th in 2021, and fell to 69th in 2026. The at-risk subfactors include security of suspects and dissidents (73), freedom of opinion and expression (105), privacy protection (86), freedom of assembly and association (115), and labor rights (66).

Hong Kong saw the shutdown of Apple Daily News and Stand News in 2021 upon the enactment of the National Security Law in 2020. The domestic Article 23 security law was enacted in March 2024 to further clamp down on “soft resistance” with the newly introduced sedition crime. Privacy rights have declined, as implementation rules for national security laws have empowered police to conduct physical searches of private property and digital devices without court warrants during national security investigations. Since 2020, NGOs, independent media outlets, and activist groups have vanished en masse amid a tightening political environment and shrinking civic space for organizational activities.
The fairly ranked subfactors are freedom from discrimination (29), rights of the accused and convicted (32), and freedom of religion (31).
Poor performance on “fundamental rights” also drags down the “open government” factor's rank (29), with its subfactor “civic participation” ranking 87 in an at-risk level.
Although Hong Kong's overall performance in civil and criminal justice remains fair, both factors have fallen from their historical high ranks of 11th and 7th to the current 20th and 23rd.
The main subfactors driving the decline in civil justice are discrimination (48) and improper government influence (56).

After the passage of Legal Aid Reforms in 2021, the number of applications to fund judicial review that challenge the government’s policy and decisions received by the Legal Aid Department dropped 60 percent from around 275 in 2016 to 110 in 2025. Of those 110 requests, the department approved only 2 cases . The overall number of judicial review cases fell from a peak of 3,899 in 2019 to 1,545 in 2022 . Because most cases involve non-refoulement claims for refugee status, the government, in addition to the administrative Unified Screening Mechanism (USM) launched in 2014, introduced a special scheme in March 2025 to appoint eligible private practitioners as Deputy Judges of the Court of First Instance to handle these cases exclusively. The mechanism disposed of more than 3700 claims in 2025. Both reforms, driven by the government administration's political considerations, have negatively affected the poor and the non-citizen's access to judicial justice in Hong Kong.
The major subfactor contributing to the fall in criminal justice ranking is “government or political influence on the criminal justice system” (61).

Hong Kong’s criminal justice ranking first plunged in 2017, from 8th to 16th, after the government labeled the civil unrest in Mong Kok , dubbed the Fishball Revolution, as a riot and reactivated the colonial-era Public Order Ordinance to prosecute protesters en masse. Then, in 2021 and 2022, the ranking dropped again amid a series of speech-related national security prosecutions against 47 pro-democracy activists for participating in the primaries of the election of the legislature for conspiracy to subvert, Apple Daily senior executives for foreign collusion , and Stand News editors for conspiracy to publish seditious content . The recent convictions and heavy sentencing of Apple Daily’s executives, including Jimmy Lai, and former leaders over collusion, Albert Ho Chun-yan, Lee Chuek-yan and Chow Hang-tung, of the now-disbanded organizer of the June 4th candlelight vigil, Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, over inciting subversion, may further downgrade the city’s criminal justice performance in the next year. The fact that all these controversial cases were handled by judges designated by the Chief Executive adds weight to the evaluation of “government or political influence on the criminal justice system”.

According to the Index’s insights, the global rule of law has declined for 9 consecutive years. Civic participation and the freedoms of speech and assembly each fell in over 60 percent of countries, and Hong Kong is among them. The city also sees the global trend of improper government influence that undermines civil and criminal justice.

The Rule of Law Index is particularly crucial to global financial centers; as the WJP notes, when the index scores reach 0.66, countries tend to have high sovereign credit ratings. Currently, Hong Kong’s score is 0.71 and trending down, while its Asian competitor, Singapore, ranks 14th with a 0.79 score and an upward trend. Watchdogs indicate this could be a bad sign for the city as it seeks to secure its spot as the region’s top economy.
